title: Dark LaTeX vs. Light LaTeX
statementMd:
In the not-so-distant future, LaTeX, the venerable typesetting system that had been a staple of academia and publishing for decades, found itself evolving into a couple of derivatives — "Dark LaTeX" and "Light LaTeX". These derivatives primarily optimized the appearance from different angles to adapt to screenless display technology.

For compatibility trial, the LaTeX lab has obtained two non-empty strings containing only lowercase English letters through analysis — the Dark LaTeX string 𝑆=𝑠1𝑠2⋯𝑠|𝑆|S=s1s2⋯s|S| and the Light LaTeX string 𝑇=𝑡1𝑡2⋯𝑡|𝑇|T=t1t2⋯t|T|, where |𝑆||S| denotes the length of 𝑆S, and |𝑇||T| denotes the length of 𝑇T. An integer quadruple (𝑝,𝑞,𝑢,𝑣)(p,q,u,v) is considered *transferrable* if and only if 1≤𝑝≤𝑞≤|𝑆|1≤p≤q≤|S|, 1≤𝑢≤𝑣≤|𝑇|1≤u≤v≤|T|, and 𝑠𝑝𝑠𝑝+1⋯𝑠𝑞𝑡𝑢𝑡𝑢+1⋯𝑡𝑣spsp+1⋯sqtutu+1⋯tv is a square string.

Your task is to help the lab find out the number of transferrable quadruples.

Recall that a square string is a string of even length in which the first half is identical to the second half. For example, "`aaaa`" and "`abcabc`" are square strings, while "`aaa`" and "`abcabd`" are not.

## Input

The input consists of two lines, where the first line contains the Dark LaTeX string 𝑆S, and the second line contains the Light LaTeX string 𝑇T.

It is guaranteed that both 𝑆S and 𝑇T consist only of lowercase English letters and their lengths do not exceed 50005000.

## Output

Output an integer in one line, indicating the number of transferrable quadruples.

## Note

In the first sample case, the transferrable quadruples are (1,1,1,1)(1,1,1,1), (1,2,1,2)(1,2,1,2), (1,3,2,2)(1,3,2,2), (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2), (2,4,1,1)(2,4,1,1), (3,3,1,1)(3,3,1,1), (3,4,1,2)(3,4,1,2), (4,4,2,2)(4,4,2,2).
